name: Powellism
summary: Powellism is the doctrine of Enoch Powell: a free-market economic liberalism (sound money, no incomes policy, no state planning, hostility to unions and corporatism) joined to a Tory belief in the absolute sovereignty of the Crown in Parliament and the organic British nation. It rejected the Common Market on sovereignty grounds, wanted Commonwealth immigration stopped and re-emigration assisted, and opposed anti-discrimination law.
scope: Powell's mature doctrine, as Hawkins (a loose set of theories, speeches and political actions prioritising economic freedom and British parliamentary sovereignty, uniting economic liberalism with traditional Toryism) and Crines, Heppell and Hill (Tory neo-liberal beliefs built on attachment to the nation state, deregulation, denationalisation and control of the money supply) describe it, taken from Powell's own parliamentary speeches 1968-1987 and the Birmingham speech of 1968. It excludes Thatcherism, Keith Joseph's later reinterpretation, and Ulster Unionist policy beyond Powell's own stated defence of the Union.

authors.quote: Camilla Schofield looks at the influence of Enoch Powell and post-war Powellism.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Hawkins presents Powellism as a prioritising of economic freedom, with the free market an 'immortal wonder' that gives maximum benefit and that state planning cannot improve; Crines describes his programme as built on deregulation and denationalisation.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Powell told the Commons in April and May 1975 that a net borrowing requirement of about £9,000 million was dangerous, that it should be nearly eliminated within two years, and that budgeting for an uncovered excess of spending 'courts inflation'.

price-stability-first.rationale: Powell called inflation the 'great destroyer' of institutions and urged the House to halt it at once, accepting the unemployment that would follow, rather than live with it.

central-planning.rationale: Hawkins records Powellism as a challenge to the planned, collective economy, where attempts to plan, control or universalise the market were a 'tilt at providence'; in 1975 Powell also called long-term public expenditure planning 'nonsense'.

state-directs-investment.rationale: On the scholarship's account Powell held that government and trade unions must not interfere with the market's allocation; state planning and interference with it was a 'tilt at providence'.

public-ownership.rationale: Crines lists denationalisation among the core commitments of Powell's Tory neo-liberalism, and Hawkins quotes him on an 'ineradicable conflict' between socialism and individual freedom.

unions-good.rationale: Hawkins reports Powell denying that trade unionism had produced any real benefits for members and treating unions as the 'vocal organs' of socialism that distort supply and demand and enslave the individual.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Powell held that collective bargaining had not raised the pay of working people and that union coercion distorted wage costs against supply and demand, though in 1975 he said it was inflation, not bargaining, that caused 'inflationary' wage rises.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Hawkins reports Powell objecting that the closed shop impinged on the individual's right of non-association.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Powell warned in 1968 that incomes policy and union-employer regulation would carry Britain 'down the road to the fascist, corporate state'; Hawkins treats opposition to corporatism and consensus as the heart of Powellism.

job-guarantee.rationale: In 1975 Powell said Britain must cut public spending and accept the unemployment that followed, and Hawkins records that he thought the pursuit of full employment must not hinder the free market.

economic-freedom.rationale: Hawkins quotes Powell that there is an 'essential and ineradicable conflict between socialism itself and the freedom of the individual under the law', and presents free markets as the condition of that freedom.

total-state.rationale: Powell called state direction of the economic life of the individual the road to 'the fascist, corporate state' and, on Hawkins's account, held that government must keep to its elementary duty of protecting individual liberty rather than rearranging society.

state-harmful.rationale: Powellism joins economic liberalism to a Toryism that upholds a sovereign Parliament, social order and the state's obligation and authority to protect its citizens.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: In 1972 Powell named the House's exclusive control over taxation and expenditure as the basis of its power built over centuries, and opposed any spending of taxes without a vote of the House.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Powell opposed the 1972 Bill because laws made and adjudicated elsewhere would override the law and courts of the realm, ending judicial independence and legislative supremacy.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Powell opposed British entry to the European Community because it would give up legislative supremacy, control of taxation and judicial independence, and he ended his 1972 speech 'It shall not pass'.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Powell held that 'no Parliament can bind its successor' and that the omnicompetence of the Crown in Parliament was the root of British democracy; Hawkins treats the sanctity of a sovereign Parliament as central to Powellism.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Powell's doctrine that every Parliament can undo what another has done, with law resting on precedent and no document or treaty binding it, is incompatible with a written bill of rights ordinary majorities cannot amend.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In 1975 Powell called the hereditary Crown the nation's unique institution, 'the common, precious and hereditary jewel', and said parliamentary government would be impossible without a hereditary monarchy of historical origin.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Powell defended the Crown as a monarchy of historical, prescriptive and hereditary origin on which parliamentary sovereignty depends.

elective-rulers.rationale: Powell held that Britain's true monarchy rests on prescription and inheritance, not on a contract or settlement, and that parliamentary sovereignty depends on that fact.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Powell defended a hereditary monarchy of prescriptive origin as the keystone of British parliamentary government, which excludes an elected head of state.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Powell called the Crown the 'symbol and personification' of the nation and the common possession of every subject, free of class.

second-chamber.rationale: In 1969 Powell opposed the Lords reform Bill as destroying a 'prescriptive Chamber' that was the nation's possession, though his objection was to the two-tier scheme more than to a second chamber as such.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Powell defended the Crown's hereditary character and the prescriptive House of Lords as inherited parts of the constitution that no generation had the right to sell off.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Powell backed renewing the Prevention of Terrorism Act as unavoidable, yet said its removal powers were 'not tolerable in a free society' other than exceptionally.

death-penalty.rationale: In 1975 Powell said he was convinced the death penalty would be no deterrent to terrorists and would be a stimulus to terrorism; Crines notes he opposed the death penalty generally.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Crines reports that Powell was sympathetic to homosexual law reform, contrary to what his pro-hanging admirers expected.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Powell accused the political class of conspiring against the people and of the 'fundamental dishonesty' of inflation, and Hawkins says he tapped discontent with the established political classes.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Powell said in 1963 that his party stood for 'neither socialism nor an inconsistent compromise with socialism, but the direct opposite', rejecting blending the best of both sides.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Hawkins describes Powell as driven by ideological certainty and principle, refusing to cling to power by borrowing opponents' policies.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: In 1983 and 1984 Powell argued that Britain's independent nuclear weapon has no rational role, since no one would use it in a last resort, and said he would sooner the power to use it were in no one's hands.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Powell told the House in 1983 that he would 'much sooner that the power to use' Britain's nuclear weapon 'was not in the hands of any individual in this country at all', and in 1984 that deterrence cannot rationally be made good.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: In 1976 Powell argued that directly elected legislative assemblies for Scotland and Wales, as national parts of the United Kingdom, force a choice between federation, separation and suppression, and so are incompatible with the unitary state.

separate-church-state.rationale: Powell held in 1984 that the Church of England is the national church only because of royal and lay supremacy, and warned the Synod against reducing that supremacy.

national-church-status.rationale: Powell said the Church of England is the church of the nation because of royal supremacy, and that a self-governing church would be a mere sect rather than the national church.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Powell defended the lay and royal supremacy over the Church of England and opposed its becoming a self-managing corporation, though he did not call for curbing church property.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: In 1975 Powell opposed the Sex Discrimination Bill in principle, objecting to the commission it created as a bureaucratic machine that would bring suspicion and discord into employment.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Powell opposed legislating equal outcomes between the sexes, holding sex differentiation to be all-pervasive and the Bill's aims a 'defiance of reality'.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Powell said sex differentiation confers advantage 'now in one direction, now in the other' and that women's gains came from removal of legal disabilities and social change, not detection of discrimination.

nation-first.rationale: Hawkins describes Powellism as 'fierce nationalism' and a defence of the sovereign nation against creeping globalisation, and in 1987 Powell asked for a foreign policy 'willed by its people', not dictated from outside.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: On Hawkins's account Powellism celebrates the organic national identity of England and Englishness, formed by precedent and an emotional attachment to inherited institutions.

gradual-change.rationale: Powell held the constitution to be evolutionary and rooted in precedent, so that tampering with it risked rebellion, though he also attacked consensus politics.

reduce-immigration.rationale: In the 1968 Birmingham speech Powell called for 'stopping, or virtually stopping, further inflow' of immigrants for settlement, which Crines identifies as his central position.

promote-ethnic-return-migration.rationale: Powell urged 'the encouragement of re-emigration' with generous assistance in 1968 and in 1970 asked the Home Secretary to implement assisted voluntary repatriation of New Commonwealth immigrants, of whom many held citizenship.

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: Powell wanted Commonwealth citizens treated on the same footing as aliens, which is not racial on its face, yet his case centred on the number of coloured immigrants and on integration across 'marked physical differences, especially of colour'.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Powell argued in 1968 that integration was a delusion for most immigrants, that numbers were of the essence, and that communalism was a canker leading to 'dangerous fragmentation within society'.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Powell said a citizen must not be denied his 'right to discriminate in the management of his own affairs between one fellow-citizen and another', nor be made to justify his motives, and voted for the Opposition's amendment against the 1968 Race Relations Bill; in 1975 he called attacking discrimination by law a 'mania' because 'all life is about discrimination'.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Powell's declared policy was that all citizens should be equal before the law with no discrimination or difference made between them by public authority.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Powell said the immigrant should not be elevated into a privileged or special class and that public authority should make no difference between citizens.

I shall tell the Minister exactly what would happen if a particular trade union, all the trade unions together, or all the income earners together were to place that limitation upon themselves, if they possibly could. Of course, it would not be practical or possible, but I accept for the purposes of the argument the hypothesis posed to me. The only consequence would be that all prices other than the price of labour would have to rise in order to take up the consequences of the increased flood of money released by the Government's inflationary financing of its expenditure. It is literally not in the power—and I am obliged to the Minister, for he enables me, finally, to make my point once again and briefly

The Minister of State, Treasury envisaged that in one period inflation would be caused by rising prices, but that when prices ceased to rise it would be caused by rising wages, not realising that, if it is basically due to an ever-increasing flow of money, when the pressure relaxes in one place it will increase in another: it will be a balloon which, if pushed in at one point, billows out at another. notes: Powellism is a loose body of positions drawn from one man's career, so the record is thin outside economics, constitution, immigration and the Union. Themes searched: economy (inflation, borrowing, unions, planning, nationalisation), government (sovereignty, Crown, Lords, Parliament, emergency powers), world (Europe, nuclear deterrent, US bases, Rhodesia), society (race, immigration, death penalty, homosexual law reform), the Church of England and the established church, devolution and the Union, sex-discrimination law, and Northern Ireland. Hawkins and Crines are scholarship on Powellism; Hawkins's later chapters on Thatcher, Joseph and the miners' strike were not used. Powell's statements on Rhodesia, the Union and Northern Ireland were read but left null where they settle no statement. Powell's Race Relations Bill vote (s12) is recorded but a reasoned amendment is not a clear vote on the principle, so it is used only as support. No source found a position for Powell on welfare, health, education, tax rates, trade tariffs, abortion, the family or the environment.
